title: 2025 Generative AI in Professional Services Report
author: Thomson Reuters Institute

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The report is consistent with the cluster’s view that AI has useful, task-specific applications but that under-resourced justice providers face disproportionate implementation and reliability risks. It materially adds evidence that limited customization, expertise and funding may force public defenders toward free or affordable models rather than systems tailored to their needs.
qs: For some, the lack of customization or ability to develop technology to assist with specific needs may be holding back broader adoption.

Small scale implementation has begun in my organization, which is a good start, but we lack the expertise and funding to push forward a proprietary system, which means we’re at the mercy of whichever models are free or affordable for us.” Among those respondents who said their organizations are using GenAI tools, use cases have not changed significantly within the past 12 months.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s augmentation-and-supervision framing and materially strengthens its organisational dimension with 2025 survey evidence showing that adoption is advancing while training, governance and ROI measurement lag. It also reinforces the need for human verification and continuing professional education, though it provides little direct evidence on apprenticeship or deskilling effects.
qs: GenAI is not a standalone technology; it operates best when symbiotically complementing professionals’ analytical and relationship-oriented skills.
Nearly two-thirds (64%), meanwhile, said they had received no GenAI training at work.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core view that GenAI is best deployed selectively as augmentation for repeatable work, with human verification retained. It materially strengthens the operating-model proposition with 2025 survey evidence showing enterprise rollout lagging expectations, weak ROI measurement, and substantial policy and training gaps, then recommends strategic alignment, governance, measurement and continuous learning.
qs: “I don’t think it replaces the person, but [rather it] requires the person to perform the rigorous thinking to what is being produced by AI.” This sentiment was reflected by a number of respondents: the growing realization that GenAI technology is not intended to replace professionals, but to augment the work that they already perform.
To truly extract value from GenAI tools, any GenAI plan needs to tie into the larger strategic objectives of an organization.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s distinction between enthusiasm and demonstrated value: it shows expected workflow centrality substantially exceeding current integration, while stressing retraining, critical review, ethical and privacy risks, and weak organisational readiness. Its cross-profession survey evidence describes adoption and expectations rather than proving investment returns.
qs: Just 13% say GenAI is central to their organization’s workflow currently, but an additional 29% believe it will be central within the next year.

Existing workforces need to be retrained about how to use, how to challenge, and how to recognize the use of generative AI, and there are also serious ethical and privacy concerns, particularly when working in the legal field.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s view that GenAI is an operating-model and client-delivery issue, not merely an internal productivity tool. It calls for firms and clients to negotiate deployment, efficiencies and cost savings, and predicts that firms delaying those discussions may lose work. Its contribution is qualitative and advisory rather than evidence of a completed market-wide bargaining shift.
qs: The next step for both sides is to determine not only how GenAI can fit in an enterprise-wide setting, but how both sides can mutually realize value from the potential efficiencies and cost savings that GenAI can bring.
Or, to put it another way, clients may not actually communicate their desires to their outside firms — they’ll simply curtail the work.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s principal proposition that adoption or usage alone does not produce productivity or strategic value. It emphasizes organisational integration, alignment with broader objectives, training and policy, and separate ROI measurement, while offering readiness and survey evidence rather than direct estimates of productivity distribution across user groups.
qs: At the same time, however, initial adoption does not necessarily equal true integration into organizations’ strategy at large.
And while most believe GenAI is imminently becoming a part of their daily workflow, only about one-third reported having a GenAI policy or receiving any kind of GenAI training at their organization.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s bounded complementarity account: respondents anticipate productivity gains and broad use while maintaining that legally trained human review, safeguards and workforce retraining remain necessary. Its low perceived job-threat figures also align with the cluster’s caution that task substitution and organisational change do not yet establish aggregate employment displacement.
qs: People need to understand that they will still need a legally trained human brain to assess documents, etc.” One US government senior policy analyst also voiced concerns about the technology’s impact, saying: “There are so many opportunities and new innovations that come with generative AI.

In actuality, however, few professionals actually said they believe that GenAI is a major threat in each of these areas — fewer than 20% of legal professionals and fewer than 10% of tax, accounting & audit professionals said they see GenAI as coming for their jobs or bottom lines.

kp.k: Survey covers 1,702 professionals familiar with GenAI
kp.d: The report draws on an online survey conducted in January and February 2025, using Thomson Reuters lists and screening for familiarity with GenAI. Respondents worked in legal, tax, accounting, audit, corporate risk, fraud and government roles, including providers and corporate departments. Countries represented were the United States (42%), Canada (15%), United Kingdom (12%), Australia (12%), Brazil (9%), New Zealand (6%), Argentina (5%) and Mexico (less than 1%). Findings concern reported practices, attitudes and expectations.
qs: The survey was done through an online survey with 1,702 respondents, conducted in January and February 2025.
The sample was drawn from lists provided by Thomson Reuters, and participants were screened to ensure that they were familiar with GenAI technology.

kp.k: Adoption increases without equivalent strategic integration
kp.d: Across professions, reported organization-wide active use rose from 12% in 2024 to 22% in 2025, while organizations with no plans to use GenAI fell from 45% to 28%. Separately, 41% reported personally using publicly available tools and 17% industry-specific tools. The report's central argument is that adoption has advanced faster than integration into organizational strategy and value measurement.
qs: Those respondents saying their organizations are already active users of GenAI increased to 22% in 2025, compared to 12% in 2024.
At the same time, the proportion who said their organizations have no plans to use GenAI dropped to just over one-quarter (28%) in 2025, from almost half (45%) in 2024.
Professionals are using GenAI, but they aren’t capitalizing on GenAI’s potential value.

kp.k: Optimism grows, but professional endorsement remains qualified
kp.d: Across the sample, 55% described themselves as excited or hopeful, an 11-percentage-point increase from 2024. Some 89% saw applications in their work, up from 81%, while 62% thought GenAI should be used. Figure 5 reports endorsement at 59% among law firms, 57% among corporate legal respondents and 48% in government. One-quarter overall had not formed a strong opinion; the report identifies accuracy, reliability and oversight as continuing reservations.
qs: more than half (55%) of respondents said they were excited or hopeful about the technology.
That represents a combined increase of 11 percentage points compared to 2024.
The majority of respondents (62%) across all represented industries said they still believe that GenAI actively should be used for their own work purposes.
there are still one-quarter of professionals who have not formed a strong opinion as to whether GenAI should be used in the workplace.

kp.k: Augmentation centers on routine work and professional judgment
kp.d: Respondents commonly expected automation of routine, low-value tasks to release time for higher-value work, rather than replace professionals. The Institute recommends managing cultural change alongside technology implementation and emphasizing analytical, relational and empathetic capabilities. Its assertion that these capabilities are not replaceable by current tools is an editorial view, not a demonstrated survey outcome.
qs: Professionals are largely looking to GenAI for routine and low-level tasks, automating work that would then free them up for more higher-value tasks.
the growing realization that GenAI technology is not intended to replace professionals, but to augment the work that they already perform.
For organizational leaders, this makes focusing on cultural change just as important as focusing on technological change for any GenAI implementation.

kp.k: Legal use spans research, review and drafting
kp.d: Among users in legal and government settings, Figure 13 reports document review at 74%, legal research at 73%, document summarization at 72% and brief or memo drafting at 59% in 2025. Six use cases reached at least 50%, indicating multiple applications among users rather than single-task adoption. Contract drafting declined slightly, which the report partly attributes to greater government representation in the sample.
qs: For respondents from law firms, corporate law departments, government legal departments, and court systems, document review and legal research still lead the way.
Notably, six separate use cases were cited by 50% or more of legal industry users.
Although that can partially be attributed to a higher proportion of government users in the sample, for whom contract drafting is not a regular use case.

kp.k: Current users incorporate GenAI into recurring work
kp.d: More than 40% of active users across professions reported at least daily use, and just under three-quarters at least weekly use. Law firm users lagged other populations slightly, but 69% still used it at least weekly. A Canadian associate suggested that faster research could enable lawyers to bill more files daily; this is an individual account of a possible business benefit, not measured productivity evidence.
qs: More than 40% of active users said they use GenAI at least daily, while just under three-quarters use GenAI at least weekly.
Law firm respondents lag slightly behind other populations among active users, although even in that case, 69% still said they use GenAI tools at least weekly.
I think it can assist lawyers conducting research, enabling lawyers to bill more files daily, as a result of spending less time on tasks.

kp.k: Other professions show task-specific adoption patterns
kp.d: In tax, accounting and audit, six applications reached at least 50% of active users. Tax research and return preparation remained leading uses; accounting and bookkeeping fell from 79% in 2024 to 57% in 2025, while tax advisory rose nine percentage points. In risk and fraud, summarization rose 27 percentage points to 82%, with risk assessment and reporting and document review exceeding two-thirds. The report distinguishes firms' marketing and business-development uses from corporate compliance and reporting uses.
qs: the proportion citing accounting and bookkeeping fell to 57% in 2025, from 79% in 2024 (when it was the top use case).
Tax advisory, meanwhile, rose nine percentage points to become the thirdmost cited use case in 2025.
In the risk & fraud space, document summarization jumped 27 percentage points in the past year to become the top use case.
Corporate professionals, meanwhile, are more likely to use GenAI for compliance and reporting purposes.

kp.d: In the wide-scale rollout results, 12% reported implementation in 2024 and another 39% expected it within 12 months, but only 26% reported wide-scale use in 2025. The report treats this gap as evidence that enterprise implementation is more complex than individual adoption. Separately, 13% said GenAI was already central to workflow, another 29% expected this within a year, and 95% expected it within five years; these are forecasts, not achieved integration.
qs: In 2024, just 12% of respondents said their organizations had conducted a wide-scale roll-out of GenAI, although an additional 39% said their organizations planned to do so within the next 12 months.
Fast forward to 2025, and now 26% reported using GenAI on a wide-scale basis
95% of all professionals believe that GenAI will be a central part of their organization’s workflow within the next five years, while just 3% believe it will never happen.

kp.k: Resource constraints limit proprietary systems and customization
kp.d: The report says few organizations have developed proprietary systems, with most relying on external technology providers. Some larger organizations have developed and productized systems, but remain a small proportion. A US public defender described funding and expertise constraints as creating dependence on free or affordable models, alongside concerns about data protection and embedded biases.
qs: Currently, few professional services organizations have invested in developing their own proprietary systems, with most instead relying on outside technology providers for their GenAI needs, according to respondents.

Small scale implementation has begun in my organization, which is a good start, but we lack the expertise and funding to push forward a proprietary system, which means we’re at the mercy of whichever models are free or affordable for us.

kp.k: Accuracy concerns preserve the need for human verification
kp.d: Respondents raised inaccurate output, hallucinations, bias, privacy and excessive reliance as barriers. A UK law firm attorney reported redrafting documents produced through ChatGPT for lay clients who could not identify omissions or errors, and argued that legally trained humans remained necessary to assess documents. A government policy analyst emphasized retraining staff to use and challenge outputs. These are practitioner concerns and experiences, not measured error rates.
qs: Others see more logistical concerns, such as the need to train wide swaths of the workforce not only on how to use the tools, but also to check for hallucinations and potential biases within the tools.

I do worry about lay clients using it, as I’ve already had to redraft many documents which were produced by ChatGPT for the purposes of lay clients who have no idea what to ask, what to include, or what is potentially incorrect in what has been generated.
People need to understand that they will still need a legally trained human brain to assess documents, etc.

kp.k: Regulatory disruption concerns exceed major employment fears
kp.d: Fewer than 20% of legal professionals and fewer than 10% of tax, accounting and audit professionals regarded GenAI as a major threat to jobs or bottom lines. The report describes stronger concerns about unauthorized practice and the performance of lawyers' work by non-lawyers or technology. It links respondents' expectations of accelerated liberalization to the UK's 2007 Legal Services Act and more limited developments in Utah and Arizona, without establishing that GenAI has caused regulatory change.
qs: fewer than 20% of legal professionals and fewer than 10% of tax, accounting & audit professionals said they see GenAI as coming for their jobs or bottom lines.
many respondents said they believe there will be a major impact on the unauthorized practice of law — the ability of non-lawyers or technology to perform the work of lawyers.
Many respondents said they believe GenAI may accelerate this timeline.
The true answer about how GenAI may impact jobs, revenue, or the profession at large may be years — if not decades — away.

kp.k: ROI measurement remains uncommon and internally focused
kp.d: Only 20% reported organizational measurement of GenAI ROI, 59% reported none and the remainder did not know. Among those measuring ROI, internal cost savings (79%), employee usage (64%) and employee satisfaction (51%) were more common metrics than client satisfaction (38%), projected external revenue (31%) or new business won (24%). The report argues that weak measurement obstructs assessment of value in client work.
qs: just 20% of respondents said their organizations were measuring the ROI of GenAI tools, while more than half (59%) said their organizations were not measuring ROI, while the remainder did not know.
of the small percentage of respondents that measure ROI, only 38% of those are actively measuring client satisfaction as well.

kp.k: Pricing expectations mix hourly continuity and alternative fees
kp.d: Across law and tax firms, 46% expected rates to remain unchanged, seven percentage points below 2024. The report links law firms' expectations of continuity to their historical billable-hour model, while reporting that 40% expected alternative fee arrangements to increase because of GenAI. Tax firms were more likely to anticipate increases: 6% significant and 37% slight, compared with 39% expecting unchanged rates. These are pricing expectations, not observed fee changes.
qs: about half (46%) of respondents in those firms said they believe GenAI will not have an impact on their rates.
this represents a 7 percentage point drop from 2024
40% of respondents said they expect the use of alternative fee arrangements to increase as a result of GenAI
many law firm practitioners expect the status quo to continue.

kp.k: Insourcing and verification may reshape law firm economics
kp.d: The report identifies corporate legal departments' potential to retain more work internally. A UK solicitor predicted the greatest negative effects for mid-tier firms whose clients could use GenAI effectively, while warning that larger firms might realize less cost reduction than expected because AI-generated material needs verification. The report separately contrasts law firms' tendency to absorb technology costs as overhead with tax firms' greater willingness to pass costs to clients.
qs: Corporate legal clients also play a role in these calculations, with the potential for keeping more work in-house than before.

likely to have the greatest negative impact in mid-tier firms whose clients have the capacity to use GenAI themselves in an effective manner. In larger firms, Gen AI will be used effectively but may not lead to the sorts of costs savings that firms and clients expect, due to the need to verify AI-generated material.
Many law firm respondents indicated that they expect to absorb GenAI costs as overhead
one-quarter of respondents noting that they plan to pass through GenAI costs across the board, and another quarter saying they plan to pass through costs on a case-by-case basis.

kp.k: Client demand outpaces visibility and explicit instructions
kp.d: A majority of clients (57%) wanted outside firms to use GenAI, yet 71% of law firm clients and 59% of tax firm clients did not know whether their firms used it. Corporate legal and tax endorsement stood at 59% and 77%, respectively. Figure 23 reports that 8% had instructed law firms to use GenAI and 10% not to; for tax firms the figures were 14% and 4%. The Institute recommends proactive conversations about usage, value, fees and preferences, warning that clients might reduce work without first articulating their demands.
qs: a majority (57%) of clients want their firms to be using GenAI — but 71% of law firm clients and 59% of tax firm clients said they did not know whether their outside firms were doing so or not.

while 77% of respondents from corporate tax departments and 59% of those from corporate law departments said they believe that GenAI should be used for client work, very few have actually included such provisions in RFPs or other guidelines for outside firms.
clients may not actually communicate their desires to their outside firms — they’ll simply curtail the work.

kp.d: Some 52% reported no workplace GenAI policy, down 14 percentage points from 2024; 70% of tax firm respondents reported no policy. The report recommends ethical-use rules and safeguards for sensitive client data. An interviewed tax partner described policy development intended to prevent client data from being accessed or compromised by AI learning models.
qs: More than half of respondents (52%) said they believed their organizations had no policies around GenAI at work, whether a standalone policy or as part of a larger technology policy.
The number of organizations without these policies did drop 14 percentage points in the last year alone
among tax firms, where 70% of respondents said their organizations did not have any sort of policy governing the use of GenAI.

kp.d: Reported GenAI training availability rose from 19% in 2024 to 31% in 2025, while 64% reported no training. Even in legal, fewer than half had been trained. Among those receiving training, approximately one-third received it less than annually or as needed, and fewer than one-quarter every few months or more frequently. The Institute recommends ongoing learning analogous to CLE or CPE because use cases, tools and business effects change rapidly.
qs: the proportion of respondents who said their organizations are engaging in some training on GenAI has increased 12 percentage points in the past year alone.
Even legal, which registers a higher training rate than other industries, has less than half of its professionals trained on GenAI tools.
One-third of respondents who said they receive training said they receive it less than annually or just as needed.
leaders need to view it less as training, and more like ongoing learning in the style of CLE or CPE.

kp.k: Hiring practices misalign with anticipated workflow transformation
kp.d: Only 2% reported that GenAI knowledge was required in hiring, with another 24% treating it as desirable but unnecessary. Uncertainty about its role in hiring rose seven percentage points to 29%; about one-third of law firm respondents did not know whether their firms considered these skills. The report warns that expecting GenAI-centered workflows without hiring or training for relevant capabilities could set new recruits up for failure.
qs: Only 2% of respondents said their organization makes GenAI knowledge a requirement in current hiring practices, although an additional 24% said they believe it is “nice to have” even if not necessary.
at 29% now, this total actually rose 7 percentage points over 2024.

some new hires may be set up for failure because they are entering organizations that say they want GenAI to be central to their workflow, but they are not hiring for those skills nor are training to provide those skills.

kp.k: Report characterizes change as evolution rather than revolution
kp.d: The Institute concludes that GenAI has not yet fundamentally disrupted professional work or firm-client interactions. It recommends moving beyond initial adoption through value measurement, responsible-use policies, training, hiring and direct client discussions. An Australian law firm attorney anticipated that the next 24 months would reveal actual effects as products entered production and clients developed demands and restrictions; this remains a respondent's forecast.
qs: GenAI has not broken the ways professionals work or significantly disrupted the interactions between firms and their clients.

This means measuring GenAI’s utility for both internal and external stakeholders, instituting policies and procedures to make sure the new technology is used ethically and responsibly, and training and hiring employees to ensure GenAI runs smoothly far into the future.
The next 24 months will be extremely telling on the impact of GenAI on the legal industry and professional work more broadly

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Institute describes expanding, predominantly augmentative adoption rather than completed disruption, while respondents anticipate changes in workflows, pricing, client sourcing and professional roles.
pts.d:
1. Adoption and workflows: The Thomson Reuters Institute reports that organization-wide GenAI use across the surveyed professions rose from 12% in 2024 to 22% in 2025; legal-sector use rose from 14% to 26%. Personal use of publicly available tools was 41%, and industry-specific tools 17%. Respondents expect much deeper integration: 13% say GenAI is already central to organizational workflows, another 29% expect this within a year, and 95% expect it within five years. These are reported adoption levels and respondent expectations, respectively.
2. Tasks and productivity: The Institute reports that document review and legal research remain leading legal/government applications, with six use cases cited by at least half of users. Respondents expect routine-task automation to release time for higher-value work. An anonymous Canadian law firm associate predicts faster research will let lawyers handle and bill more files daily. Across professions, respondents anticipate efficiency, cost reduction and improved quality, rather than reporting measured gains.
3. Augmentation rather than replacement: The Institute argues that GenAI complements analytical and relationship skills and does not currently replace professionals' complex reasoning, client understanding or interpersonal strengths. It concludes that adoption has so far been evolutionary rather than significantly disruptive to firm-client interactions. An anonymous UK CEO offers a broader forecast that higher-level skills can now be automated, while emphasizing guardrails.
4. Jobs and market boundaries: Fewer than 20% of legal respondents regard GenAI as a major threat to jobs or firm finances. Respondents nevertheless see greater threat around unauthorized practice of law; the Institute reports their belief that GenAI may accelerate legal-market liberalization. This is a perception about future market boundaries, not evidence that regulation has changed because of AI.
5. Pricing and costs: Forty percent of respondents to the relevant pricing question expect alternative fee arrangements to increase because of GenAI. Many law firm respondents nevertheless expect rate stability: Figure 19 reports 53% expecting unchanged rates. Forty-two percent of law firm respondents expect GenAI costs to be absorbed as overhead. Tax firms differ: 43% expect rates to rise, and roughly half intend to pass technology costs to clients either generally or case by case. These are projections, not observed AI-caused price changes.
6. Insourcing and competitive exposure: The Institute identifies the possibility that corporate legal departments will retain more work internally. An anonymous UK solicitor predicts the greatest adverse impact on mid-tier firms whose clients can use GenAI effectively, and cautions that verification may limit savings in larger firms. The Institute also warns that clients may curtail assignments without first explicitly requiring AI adoption.
7. Client relationships and unrealized value: Fifty-seven percent of surveyed clients want outside firms to use GenAI, including 59% of corporate legal respondents, but 71% of law firm clients do not know whether their firms use it. The Institute argues that weak communication and limited ROI measurement obstruct value realization and informed pricing discussions.
8. Reliability and capability-building: An anonymous UK law firm attorney reports redrafting documents generated for lay clients and argues that legally trained humans remain necessary to assess output. The Institute maintains that ethical, useful integration requires governance, ongoing learning and attention to implementation culture. It warns that organizations expecting AI-centered workflows without training or hiring for relevant skills may set new recruits up for failure.
9. Cross-domain implications: An anonymous US tax firm director describes AI productivity gains as critical to sustaining capacity amid costly talent, fewer entrants and client pressure for value. An anonymous Australian corporate risk manager predicts reduced low-value work and shorter time from identifying problems to delivering value. The Institute reports expanded risk/fraud use of summarization, but its proposed explanation involving new US regulations is interpretation rather than a demonstrated causal result.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source primarily supplies self-reported survey findings, supplemented by anonymous practitioner experience and the Institute's strategic interpretations; it does not establish productivity or displacement effects through performance testing.
pts.d:
The evidence base is an online survey of 1,702 professionals conducted in January–February 2025, drawn from Thomson Reuters lists and screened for familiarity with GenAI. Respondents came from legal, tax/accounting/audit, corporate risk/fraud and government organizations across eight countries, with 42% in the United States. Overall percentages therefore describe this cross-professional sample rather than lawyers alone. The report compares results with its 2024 survey; it does not establish that the same individuals or organizations were followed over time. Indeed, it notes that a larger government share partly explains lower contract-drafting usage and may affect hiring responses.
Adoption, frequency, task use, policies and training are survey reports about current practice. Workflow forecasts, rate projections and threat assessments are respondents' expectations or beliefs. Task-use percentages concern users, not all professionals: among active users, more than 40% report daily use and just under three-quarters weekly use; 69% of law firm users report at least weekly use. Aggregate legal/government use cases include document review at 74% and legal research at 73%.
The UK attorney's report of correcting lay-client documents is individual experience supporting the need for human verification; it is not a measured hallucination rate or a court-sanctions case. The Canadian associate's productivity claim, UK solicitor's market-segment forecast and tax director's sustainability claim are practitioner views without quantified outcome studies. The Institute's claims about non-replaceable professional strengths, client attrition and the need for strategic integration are editorial analysis. Historical references to the UK's Legal Services Act and Utah/Arizona reforms provide context, not evidence that AI has accelerated liberalization. A separate 2025 legal-market report is cited for rising law firm rates, not to establish that AI caused those increases.
The report itself highlights limited measurement: only 20% say their organizations measure GenAI ROI, 59% say they do not and 21% do not know. Among those measuring ROI, internal cost savings are the most commonly tracked metric at 79%, while 38% track client satisfaction. These figures describe measurement practices, not demonstrated savings or satisfaction improvements. No model benchmark, controlled productivity study or observed AI-caused job-loss estimate is offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report combines early-2025 observations, near-term rollout expectations and a five-year workflow forecast, while explicitly leaving long-run employment and revenue effects unresolved.
pts.d:
Current-state findings refer to the January–February 2025 survey, with adoption and sentiment comparisons to 2024. Respondents' five-year workflow horizon runs approximately to 2030; 34% anticipate centrality within one to two years. More than 60% say their organizations have already begun wide-scale rollout or plan it within a year. However, the report distinguishes aspiration from implementation: in 2024, 12% reported wide-scale use and a further 39% expected rollout within 12 months, whereas only 26% reported wide-scale use in 2025. It interprets this as evidence that enterprise integration is more complex than individual adoption, rather than presenting projected adoption as certain.
An anonymous Australian law firm attorney identifies the next 24 months as particularly revealing as products enter production and clients develop demands and restrictions. The Institute separately says effects on jobs, revenue and the profession may take years or decades to become clear. Its assertion that core professional strengths are not replaceable is explicitly framed around current capability.
Expected benefits are conditional on safe, accurate and context-appropriate use; human checking; adequate governance and continuing training; cultural adaptation; alignment with organizational strategy; ROI measurement; and firm-client agreement about value. The UK solicitor's predicted mid-tier exposure depends on clients having effective GenAI capability, while the anticipated savings shortfall in large firms depends on verification demands. An anonymous US public defender identifies funding, expertise, data protection and bias as constraints on moving beyond small-scale implementation. The Institute's warning about recruitment is conditional on organizations neither selecting for AI skills nor developing them despite planning AI-centered workflows.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects differ between service providers and corporate buyers, between firm sizes, and between well-resourced organizations and public-service or lay users.
pts.d:
Lawyers and other professionals are expected to spend less time on repeatable tasks and more on higher-value analysis and relationships, while retaining responsibility for checking output. New hires face a potential skills mismatch: only 2% of respondents report GenAI knowledge as a hiring requirement and 24% call it desirable; 64% report no workplace GenAI training. Firm leaders face implementation, governance, pricing and client-communication decisions rather than software adoption alone.
Law firms may face pressure to adjust fee arrangements, absorb technology costs and demonstrate benefits to clients. The UK solicitor singles out mid-tier firms serving AI-capable clients as especially vulnerable to insourcing, while forecasting that large firms' verification burden can constrain cost savings. Corporate legal departments are buyers who may retain additional work internally and seek more competitive outside fees; their enterprise savings are distinct from access-to-justice outcomes.
